en: A Song on the Mutual Support of Samādhi and Prajñā.

Within the essential teachings of the Patriarchs, there are two gates. The ten perfections and myriad practices are called supreme. The first, named "Cessation and Contemplation," assists those who are newly learning;
the latter becomes the root of samādhi, prajñā, and bodhi. Though it is a single dharma, it appears as a dual division; the nature of dharmas is quiescent, its essence true.

Cessation (*śamatha*) is quiescent yet constantly illuminating; wondrous contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) abides therein. With concentration as father and wisdom as mother, they can conceive the gateway to the thousand sages.
They increase the power of the faculties and nourish the holy embryo, giving birth in every thought-moment to the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Concentration is the general and wisdom is the minister;
together they assist the Mind-King to achieve the Unsurpassed, eternally serving as the gate for all sentient beings to realize the Way. This is the Bodhi of the ancient Buddhas.
It is like the moonlight shining forth, extinguishing the evil stars of the non-Buddhists; it can lift the torch of wisdom until it shines ever more clearly.
It nourishes the sprouts of the Way and removes the knots of craving. Wisdom is like the sun’s radiance, shattering the dark chamber of ignorance.

It can cause the meditations of ignorant people with false views to be fully transformed into the *prajñāpāramitā*. For a short while, remain silent and still for a single *kṣaṇa*, and gradually increase your cultivation.
One achieves perfect realization; for all the sages, the merit compared is not great. Ultimately, one beholds the wondrous nature of the numinous mind-palace (*lingtai*).

Upon hearing the Dharma but briefly as it passes the ear, the seeds of awakening are infused into the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and arise. With a single thought of turning the light inward, right wisdom opens.

To achieve Buddhahood in such a brief moment—this is the inconceivable meaning of the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bala*). Transforming the ordinary into the holy occurs in an instant. Boundless beings...

The faculty of death is severed; the nests of afflictions accumulated over kalpas are demolished. The water of the profound mind is pure and the intent is serene. Its light swallows the ten thousand forms and illuminates the myriad paths.
Having gouged open one’s own eyes, they are free from flaw or obscuration. Originally, within the three realms, not a single dharma can bind.

The thieves of discursive thought and observation are subdued at once; the malady of clinging to conditions is suddenly cleansed. Washing away the grime of conceptualization and scrubbing the dust of delusion, the Dharma-body is revealed.
Ah, firm is the life-force of wisdom! Like a mountain severed or an ocean stilled, though heaven overturns and earth submerges, it never changes.
Luminous as lapis lazuli, it contains the jewel-moon; suddenly it has no abode and nothing to depend upon. The wisdom of *prajñā* cannot be measured;
naturally, the light of the mind manifests wherever it is. Among the gates of the myriad practices, it is the foremost guide; at all times, it is called the Dharma King. Exhausting suffering...
The ocean shatters the mountains of heterodoxy; clouds of delusion are rolled away in a single moment. Gold suddenly appears within the hut of the poor woman;
the jewel on the warrior’s forehead is restored in secret. He severs the net of ignorance and cuts the stream of desire; the Great Hero’s majestic power is peerless.

He can cause the iron bed and copper pillar to grow cold, and instantly brings to rest the karmic fruits of demonic enmity. He reconciles disputes and establishes filial piety and righteousness, manifesting everywhere.

The wisdom of all Buddhas is the destination for the myriad beings; those with biased, heterodox, and evil intellects all turn toward it as their source. From the smallest ant to the great Kunpeng, all receive the prediction of enlightenment.

If one cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*) alone, it is purely yin: things rot and one’s true livelihood is hollowed out. If one uses right wisdom to illuminate *dhyāna*, then by nature all phenomena will be as clear as a mirror.
If one cultivates wisdom alone, it is purely yang: things wither and one becomes muddled and stagnant. One must rely on wondrous concentration to assist the gate of contemplation.

Like the moon clearly manifesting once the mist and clouds are cleared, I exhort you to study equally and not practice with partiality. From the beginning, they have been of one essence without two heads;

like the two wings of a bird soaring through the realm of space, or like the two wheels of a chariot drawing a white ox, one immediately proceeds from the path of ordinary beings to the shore of enlightenment, and thus sails the boat of compassion across the ocean of karma.
Whether it be through the fixed regulations of phenomena, there is nowhere that is not perfected; or whether it be through principle...

In meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one should simply observe the nature of the mind directly below. Alternatively, in the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), one clearly perceives the arising of all dharmas through analytical calculation.

Or, in the contemplation of principle (*tattva*), one suddenly realizes that there is neither "this shore" nor "the other shore. Concentration is itself wisdom; it is neither one nor two, and is beyond mental reckoning.

Wisdom is itself concentration; they are neither identical nor distinct, transcending both observation and hearing. Or, when the two are unified, it is illumination within stillness, penetrating the true teaching. Or, when both are present...

Vanishing, it is neither concentration nor wisdom, transcending ordinary standards. When a single mote of dust enters samādhi, all motes of dust arise; within the gateway of Prajñā, this becomes the natural law (*dharmatā*).
When the body of a youth is in samādhi, the body of an old man speaks the true track. Being able to contemplate one realm, ten thousand realms are identical;
from nearby dust to distant lands, there is nothing that is not penetrated. On the path of True Suchness (*tathatā*), they discuss birth and death; in the ocean of ignorance...

The inner performance manifests the Perfect Teaching: the faculty of sight can perform the Buddha-work of the nose; when the object of form enters meditative concentration, the fragrance of the object arises.
Mind and environment are always identical, yet one constantly perceives their differences. Who says that the waves do not cultivate themselves into water?

Neither quiescent nor illuminating, it transcends words and thought; yet both quiescent and illuminating, its efficacy is peerless. Expedient means and ultimate truth proceed together to reveal the correct path; essence and function further support one another, embodying the wondrous intent.

I exhort you, my sons, not to waste this time in vain; the passing of moments is like a swift arrow or a flowing river. Mental distraction arises entirely from a lack of the gateway of meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
ignorance and blindness stem solely from a deficiency in true wisdom (*jñāna*). Let these words of truth enter your ears; ten thousand sutras and myriad treatises bear the same mark.

Never for a moment forget the full power of concentration and wisdom. In a single thought, one may suddenly return to the ground of true awakening. One must practice concentration and cultivate wisdom through hearing the Dharma;

do not allow that single point of the numinous mind to become obscured. From a tiny sprout grows a tree that embraces both arms; through the power of gradual accumulation, one becomes a Venerable Treasure.
By practicing concentration, the monkey was reborn in the heavenly realms; by a mere thought, the woman entered the Gate of the Way. This is the cause for benefiting oneself and others.
The fruition is complete; were it not for concentration and wisdom, nothing could be discussed.
